label: Curvature: The Obstruction to Flatness
notes: This chapter, printed pages 193 through 224, introduces curvature as the precise local obstruction preventing a Riemannian manifold from being Euclidean. We motivate the Riemann tensor through the failure of second covariant derivatives to commute and preview the contractions, symmetries, and sectional invariants developed across the unit.

label: Second Covariant Derivatives Do Not Commute
notes: On Euclidean space mixed partials commute, but a general connection breaks this symmetry. The curvature endomorphism measures the defect when the order of covariant differentiation is swapped along two directions, including a correction for the Lie bracket of the vector fields involved.

label: The Riemann Curvature Tensor
notes: We package the commutator defect into a multilinear map that is tensorial in all three arguments. Tensoriality means curvature depends only on pointwise vector values, not on extensions, which is why it qualifies as a genuine tensor field rather than a differential operator.

label: Flat Manifolds
notes: A manifold is flat when its curvature tensor vanishes identically. The central theorem states that vanishing curvature is equivalent to being locally isometric to Euclidean space, so the Riemann tensor is exactly the obstruction to finding flat coordinate charts around each point.

label: Parallel Transport and Holonomy
notes: Curvature manifests geometrically as holonomy: transporting a vector around a small closed loop returns it rotated by an angle proportional to the enclosed area times curvature. On a flat manifold transport is path independent, so every loop returns the vector unchanged.

label: Symmetries of the Curvature Tensor
notes: The covariant four-tensor obeys antisymmetry in the first pair, antisymmetry in the second pair, and symmetry under exchange of the two pairs. These algebraic identities drastically cut the number of independent components and underpin every later contraction and decomposition we perform.

label: The Bianchi Identities
notes: The first, algebraic Bianchi identity cyclically permutes three arguments to zero. The second, differential Bianchi identity constrains the covariant derivative of curvature and, after contraction, forces the Einstein tensor to be divergence free, a fact central to general relativity.

label: Sectional Curvature
notes: Sectional curvature assigns a number to each tangent two-plane, recovering the Gaussian curvature of the surface swept by geodesics tangent to that plane. The full set of sectional curvatures determines the entire Riemann tensor, making this scalar function a complete curvature invariant.

label: The Sign of Sectional Curvature
notes: Positive sectional curvature makes nearby geodesics converge, as on a sphere where meridians meet at the poles. Negative curvature makes them diverge exponentially, as on a saddle. Zero curvature keeps geodesic spacing linear, exactly the Euclidean behavior of parallel lines.

label: Ricci Curvature
notes: The Ricci tensor is the trace of the curvature endomorphism over one slot, a symmetric two-tensor measuring average sectional curvature through a direction. It controls how the volume of small geodesic balls deviates from the Euclidean value and drives comparison theorems later in the book.

label: Scalar Curvature
notes: Scalar curvature contracts the Ricci tensor fully against the metric, producing a single function on the manifold. It captures the leading volume distortion of small geodesic balls relative to Euclidean balls and serves as the integrand of the Einstein-Hilbert action in physics.

label: Curvature Invariants: Recap
notes: We close by tracing the contraction ladder from the full Riemann tensor down through Ricci and scalar curvature, recalling that flatness, holonomy, and sectional sign are three faces of one obstruction. The notebook checks these invariants symbolically to keep the constructions honest.
